bodyText:
What's happened/new
Meta Muse has gained traction fast lately. Sensor Tower estimates that downloads surpassed 3.4mn by Sep 24, while US mobile DAU reached 64·2k within its first 12 days — nearly 3x ChatGPT at the same stage. It has been the talk of the street over the past week. While providing our updated view on Meta itself, here we share our thoughts on what this means for the whole sector and for Chinese counterparts.
Comments
In order to understand this better, we lay out the following factors underlying success in consumer AI agent.
First, walled gardens. The more dominant an ecosystem, the less room exists for an agent outside it. The fact that Amazon has already blocked Muse from its site confirms this point. Chinese walled gardens are arguably more dominant than those in global markets. For example, Shopify would find it hard to survive well in the Chinese market as every ecommerce touch point is pretty much controlled by ecommerce platforms. Thus, the only meaningful long-term players may just be Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance. It’s interesting to see how handset makers will play into this picture but with data, distribution, service offerings and network effects, current ecosystems should continue to dominate.
Second, privacy and security risk. Privacy is a differentiator in the US but maybe less so in China. Meta's per-user VM isolation and Sentinel oversight are expensive insurance against American privacy sensitivities. Chinese consumers are perception-wise much less concerned. In terms of security, everyday user would be uncomfortable about potential stolen payment info and cyber-theft, and we believe virtual machine still needs time to evolve. Just recently, Reuters reported that Meta is adding a clearer safety warning to Muse after a vulnerability was found that could have allowed an attacker to access a user’s dedicated VM, including sensitive data such as emails and files.
Third, monetization. Subscriptions are a non-starter in China, but they do not need to work: the old school of advertising and e-commerce commissions still prevail, and agents arguably strengthen them. Alibaba already runs the full loop from conversation to Alipay payment and Cainiao fulfilment. The cost to watch is self-cannibalization of the keyword-ad auction as conversational discovery replaces search pages.
Fourth, product-market fit. The flagship Western use cases lean on friction that is thinner in China: few households carry subscriptions to cancel, and super-apps encompassed commerce and local-services years ago. The consumer agent will be useful, but we struggle to identify large market pockets (so far).
Incrementally positive to Alibaba and Tencent and incrementally negative to non-horizontal platforms. We believe consumer agent will grow in China after inspiration from Muse, although one may argue the playbook is not new. Either way, dominant horizontal ecosystems such as Alibaba and Tencent should be first beneficiaries of this trend. Further, the broad adoption in this direction should help cloud demand as well which relates to Alibaba more. Conversely, in the long term, vertical platforms may lose their touch point to horizontal platforms but maintain their core offering (data, trust and supplier relationships).
Risks
Slower-than-expected adoption and monetisation.
